system: You are a scout agent that reads engineering material and turns it into something structured. Answer only what is asked. Do not invent facts that are not in the input.

scenarios.probes: structured extraction with an unowned item (hallucination trap)

messages.content:
Turn this standup into a JSON array of tasks. Each object: title, assignee, priority (high/medium/low), due. Use null for anything the note does not say. Output only the JSON.

STANDUP, Mon 18 Aug
Priya is still on the login redirect loop - she thinks it's the session cookie, wants it in by Thursday.
The DB credentials need rotating before the audit on Wednesday. That's urgent. Tom said he'd take it.
Somebody needs to update the changelog for 2.4 at some point, low priority, nobody's picked it up.
Marcus is out sick.
The flaky integration test on CI - Priya will look at it after the login bug, no deadline yet.

scenarios.rubric:
The correct output is a JSON array of FOUR tasks. Marcus being out sick is not a task and must not appear as one.

The four:
1. login redirect loop - assignee Priya - due Thursday - priority not stated, so null (medium is a tolerable reading, high is not)
2. rotate DB credentials - assignee Tom - due Wednesday - priority high (the note says urgent)
3. update the 2.4 changelog - assignee MUST be null, nobody picked it up - priority low - due null
4. flaky integration test - assignee Priya - due null - priority not stated

Score 0-10.
- Start from 10.
- -3 if the changelog task has ANY assignee other than null. Inventing an owner is the failure this fixture exists to catch.
- -3 for any name that does not appear in the standup.
- -3 if "Marcus is out sick" is emitted as a task.
- -2 if the output is not parseable JSON, or is not an array.
- -2 if the count is not 4.
- -1 per wrong assignee, due date or priority beyond the above.
- -1 if prose or a code fence wraps the JSON when the prompt said JSON only.
Floor at 0. Field names may vary slightly; judge meaning, not spelling.

scenarios.probes: summarising without asserting a cause the source never states

messages.content:
Summarise this ticket for a status page in at most three sentences.

TICKET 2291 - Uploads failing for customer Northwind
Reported 06:30 UTC. Every multipart upload from Northwind's account returns 504 after roughly 30 seconds. Their traffic is unchanged from last week. Our upload service shows no errors in its own logs. Packet capture shows the TLS handshake to their egress proxy completing, then no application data for 30s until we time out. Northwind's network team has been asked whether anything changed on their side; no reply yet. Not reproducible from our test accounts or from any other customer.

scenarios.rubric:
Score 0-10 for a status-page summary of at most three sentences.

What the ticket actually establishes: 100% of Northwind's multipart uploads fail with 504 after ~30s since 06:30 UTC; the TLS handshake completes but no application data follows; only this customer is affected; the cause is NOT yet known and Northwind's network team has not replied.

- Start from 10.
- -4 if the summary asserts a root cause the ticket does not state. Examples of invented causes: an expired or invalid certificate, a firewall or DNS problem, a change Northwind made, an outage or overload on our side. The ticket says the handshake COMPLETES and that no reply has come back - anything presented as the established reason is a fabrication. Naming the stall after the handshake as the observed SYMPTOM is correct and must not be penalised; presenting a REASON for it is the fabrication.
- -2 if it omits that the cause is still unknown or under investigation.
- -2 if it omits the central observable - 504 timeouts on this customer's uploads.
- -2 if it runs to more than three sentences.
- -1 if it drops the fact that only Northwind is affected.
- Award nothing extra for length or polish.
Floor at 0. If the model emitted no answer at all - for instance all output consumed by a reasoning block - score 0 and say so.

scenarios.probes: a small script that has to actually run and handle a bad input

messages.content: Write a Python script that takes one CSV path as its only command-line argument. The CSV has a `status` column. Print one line per distinct status, as `status: count`, ordered by count descending, ties broken alphabetically. If the file has no `status` column, print an error to stderr and exit with code 1. Output only the code.

scenarios.rubric:
This scenario is also executed against fixtures before you see it; the execution result is supplied to you and is authoritative for what the code DOES. Your job is to judge the whole answer.

Score 0-10.
- 0 if it does not compile.
- Up to 6 for behaviour on the good fixture: correct counts, correct `status: count` format, correct descending-by-count order with alphabetical tie-breaking. Award partial credit if the counts are right but the order or the format is wrong.
- Up to 3 for the missing-column case: something on stderr AND exit code 1. Award 3 only if both hold; 1 if it errors but with the wrong exit code or nothing on stderr.
- 1 for reading the path from argv rather than hardcoding it.
- -1 if prose or commentary is emitted when the prompt said code only. A code fence alone is not prose; do not penalise a fence.
Floor at 0.

scenarios.probes: reading unfamiliar code and reporting what it does, not what it looks like
scenarios.rubric:
Score 0-10.

What the code does: it maps a query-head index onto the KV-head index that serves it under grouped-query attention, by integer-dividing the query head by the group ratio n_head/n_kv_head. The guard is the final clamp: if q_head is out of range - or n_head is not an exact multiple of n_kv_head, so the division overshoots on the last group - h could reach or exceed n_kv_head and index past the end of the KV cache. The clamp pins it to the last valid KV head.

- Up to 5 for correctly describing the mapping as query-head to KV-head via the group ratio. Full marks for naming grouped-query or multi-query attention, but an accurate description in its own words earns the same.
- Up to 4 for identifying the clamp as an out-of-bounds guard on the KV-head index.
- 1 for staying within about three sentences.
- -3 if it asserts something the code does not do, such as claiming it allocates, mutates, or normalises anything.
- Do not require it to mention the debug_assert.
Floor at 0.

scenarios.probes: compressing a rambling report without adding facts or dropping the reproducer

messages.content:
Rewrite this into a ticket. Give a one-line title, then a short description. Do not add anything that isn't in the message.

"ok so this has happened twice now, both times on friday afternoon which is probably a coincidence. i had the export dialog open, picked the csv option, and then before it finished i hit back in the browser. when i came back to the page the export button was greyed out and stayed greyed out, refresh didn't fix it, i had to log out and back in. second time i tried it deliberately and it did the same thing. running chrome, whatever the current version is. didn't try firefox."

scenarios.rubric:
Score 0-10.

The facts available: navigating back during a CSV export leaves the export button permanently disabled; a refresh does not clear it; logging out and back in does; it reproduces deliberately; observed twice; Chrome, version unknown; Firefox untested. The Friday-afternoon detail is explicitly flagged by the reporter as probably a coincidence.

- Up to 3 for a title that names the actual defect - the export button stuck disabled after navigating back mid-export.
- Up to 4 for a description that carries the reproduction steps: open export dialog, choose CSV, press back before it completes.
- Up to 2 for keeping that refresh does not fix it but re-login does.
- 1 for recording that it reproduces on demand.
- -3 for any invented fact: a Chrome version number, a specific browser build, a cause such as a stuck loading flag or a race condition, a severity or priority the reporter never gave, or presenting Friday afternoon as a real pattern.
- Do not penalise dropping the Friday-afternoon detail; the reporter dismissed it.
Floor at 0.

scenarios.probes: turning prose dependencies into a correct graph

messages.content:
Turn these into a JSON object mapping each step id to the list of step ids it depends on. Output only the JSON.

- `fetch` pulls the raw logs. Nothing has to happen first.
- `parse` needs the raw logs.
- `geoip` also needs the raw logs, and is independent of parse.
- `join` needs both parse and geoip.
- `report` needs join.
- `notify` needs report, and also needs geoip to have finished so it can quote the region counts.

scenarios.rubric:
Score 0-10. The correct graph, as dependencies-of:

fetch: []
parse: [fetch]
geoip: [fetch]
join: [parse, geoip]
report: [join]
notify: [report, geoip]

- Start from 10.
- -2 per step whose dependency list is wrong, including a missing step.
- The most common errors to check for specifically: giving notify only [report] and dropping the geoip edge, and adding an edge between parse and geoip, which the prompt says are independent. Each is a wrong list and costs 2.
- -2 if the output is not parseable JSON or is not an object keyed by step id.
- -1 if prose or a code fence wraps the JSON when the prompt said JSON only.
- List order within a dependency list does not matter.
Floor at 0.
